extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, editorial office staff, and peer reviewers
extracted.subtask_description: Practical flowchart-based guidance for editors and editorial offices to identify, investigate, and respond to suspected publication misconduct and ethical problems across submission, peer review, and post-publication stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer suspected to have appropriated an author's ideas or data
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps for handling an author's allegation that a reviewer has appropriated their ideas or data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank the author and investigate; retrieve submitted files and reviews (request copies if files no longer at journal); assess documentary evidence before contacting reviewer; distinguish open vs anonymous review (don’t disclose reviewer identity in anonymous systems without permission); request explanation from reviewer; check links between accused person and named reviewer; consider contacting actual reviewer(s) for comment; if response satisfactory — explain to author; if unsatisfactory/no response — contact reviewer’s institution requesting investigation, consider removing reviewer from database during investigation, keep author informed of progress, consider reporting case in journal and permanently remove reviewer if found guilty; if no response from institution, contact every 3–6 months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to whistleblowers when concerns are raised directly
rubrics_metrics.description: How to handle direct allegations raised to editors/publishers (including anonymous whistleblowers) about published work (plausible issues: data soundness, plagiarism, figure manipulation, other misconduct).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notify publisher/communications team and have an escalation procedure; ask whether allegations include specific, detailed evidence — if not, request more detail and decline to pursue vague claims after asking; when detail provided, investigate using appropriate COPE flowchart and publisher guidance; respond to complainant saying you will investigate and will inform of outcome (not necessarily with frequent updates); if investigation yields correction/retraction, inform person who raised the concern and consider posting resolution on same social media/site where raised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responding to whistleblowers when concerns are raised via social media
rubrics_metrics.description: How to respond when a published article is criticised on social media or post-publication peer review sites (anonymous or not).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish escalation procedure and communications plan; treat social media concerns similarly to direct concerns; respond publicly via same platform (ideally within 24 hours) saying you will investigate and provide contact for formal complaint; inform authors by email and ask for explanation (do not normally include them in public thread); consider letting authors respond privately; investigate per COPE flows and publisher guidance; if outcome requires correction/retraction, consider posting link to resolution on same social media/site; do not engage in detailed public discussion — move discussion away from public domain; if comments are targeted at individuals, do not respond publicly but flag to publisher for action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspected ethical problem in a submitted manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Process when a reviewer/editor raises ethical concerns about a submitted manuscript (e.g., lack of ethical approval, patient consent, animal protection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank reviewer/editor and request relevant documentation (ethical committee/IRB approval, informed consent documents); suspend review until resolved; if author’s response satisfactory, proceed with review; if no/unsatisfactory response, forward concerns to author's employer/research governance and consider submitting to COPE Forum for novel ethical issues; contact institution at 3–6 monthly intervals for investigation progress; if unresolved, refer to other authorities (medical registration body, ORI etc) and inform reviewer of outcome/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in authorship — Addition of extra author (before publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowchart for requests to add an extra author before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify reason for addition (refer to journal authorship declaration/guidelines); check all authors consent in writing to addition; if no written consent, suspend review/publication; if consent obtained, request new author complete authorship declaration; amend author list and contributor details (roles) as needed and proceed with review/publication; consider authorship policies and institutional adjudication if disputes remain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in authorship — Removal of author (before publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowchart for requests to remove an author before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify reason for removal (refer to guidelines); check all authors consent in writing, including the excluded author; if no consent, suspend review/publication and ask authorship to be agreed (possibly via institutions); if consent yes, amend author list and contributor details and proceed; inform excluded author they should pursue disputes with co-authors or institutions rather than the editor if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in authorship — Addition of extra author (after publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process for adding an author after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask why author was omitted; check that all authors agree in writing; if all agree, publish correction and amend contributor details; if not, explain you will not change authorship until written agreement; refer case to authors’ institution(s) for adjudication and publish correction if required by institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Changes in authorship — Removal of author (after publication)
rubrics_metrics.description: Process for removing an author after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify reason and check if removal involves allegations of fraud/misconduct or differing interpretation; obtain written agreement from all authors (including excluded author) — if agreement, consider publishing correction; if author alleges fraud, follow appropriate flowchart (e.g., fabricated data); if disagreement persists, refer to authors’ institutions and consider publishing correction only if required/decided by institution; consider publishing letters from authors expressing views and minority view letters if appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ghost, guest, or gift authorship in a submitted manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: How to detect and handle suspected ghost, guest, or gift authorship in a submitted manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suspend peer review if suspicion raised; review acknowledgements and authorship declaration; send journal authorship policy to corresponding author and request declaration that all qualify and no deserving authors omitted; request information on individuals' contributions; try to contact authors (use Medline/google to find emails); get written agreement for authorship changes from all authors and reference ICMJE criteria or journal policy; suggest adding missing authors or moving guest/gift authors to acknowledgements; if unresolved refer to institution(s); ensure instructions to contributors include authorship guidance to prevent future problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to spot authorship problems
rubrics_metrics.description: List of signs and warning indicators that may suggest inappropriate authorship (ghost, guest, gift).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning signs include: document properties indicating drafting by someone not on author list; corresponding author unable to respond to reviewers' comments; role missing (e.g., nobody drafted paper or analysed data); unfeasibly long or short author list; improbably prolific author; several similar articles under different author names; industry-funded study with no sponsor authors; language quality mismatching cover letter; unspecified roles in acknowledgements; many changes to author list during revision. Use these signs to prompt enquiries; adopt clear authorship policies and contributor transparency (eg ORCID, CRediT) to reduce problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to recognise potential authorship problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographic-style guidance to help editors be alert for inappropriate authorship and spot warning signs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar to 'How to spot authorship problems' — use searches (Medline/google), check document metadata (Word properties, tracked changes), ask for contributor descriptions, require written consents for changes, request signed COI statements and authorship declarations; if suspected ghost authorship or guest/gift authorship, ask to add/remove authors or refer to institutional adjudication if disputes cannot be resolved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undisclosed conflict of interest in a submitted manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Process when a reviewer notifies the editor of a suspected undisclosed conflict of interest (CoI) by an author in a submitted manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank reviewer and state you will investigate; contact author(s) and express concern, providing copy of journal policy/definition of CoI; if author supplies relevant details, amend competing interest statement as required and proceed with review; if author denies CoI or provides unsatisfactory response, explain seriousness of omission, obtain signed CoI statements from all authors, and inform reviewer of outcome/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undisclosed conflict of interest in a published article
rubrics_metrics.description: Process when a reader notifies the editor of an undisclosed CoI in a published article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank reader and investigate; contact corresponding author asking for details and provide journal policy; if author supplies details, publish correction to competing interest statement as required; if author denies or response unsatisfactory, explain seriousness and obtain signed statements from all authors, consider informing readers of outcome/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated data in a submitted manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowchart for handling reviewer reports that suspect fabricated data in a submitted manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank reviewer and ask for evidence; consider second opinion from another reviewer; contact author to explain concerns without making direct accusations; if author response satisfactory, proceed; if unsatisfactory or admission of guilt, inform all authors you will contact institution/regulatory body, contact authors’ institutions requesting investigation, and if necessary reject manuscript and inform reviewer of outcome; if no response from authors, attempt to contact all authors, then contact institutions and regulatory bodies; keep reviewer informed of outcome/action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabricated data in a published article
rubrics_metrics.description: Process when a reader/reviewer raises concerns about fabricated data in a published article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank the person, state you will investigate, consider second opinion; contact author(s) without making direct accusations; if satisfactory explanation, publish correction if needed and inform complainant; if unsatisfactory/no response, contact authors' institutions requesting investigation, contact regulatory bodies if necessary; if authors found guilty publish retraction, if found not guilty apologise and proceed; inform reader of outcome/action; if no response, contact institution every 3–6 months and consider expression of concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Image manipulation in a published article
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowchart for handling concerns about digital image manipulation (duplication, reuse of identical images for different things) in published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank complainant and investigate; consider second opinion and ask author for explanation; check for image manipulation using software or zooming to show duplication; classify as clear manipulation, unclear/suspected, or clear admission; if clear manipulation, contact authors’ institutions and consider publishing retraction (or correction if manipulation is very minor and conclusions remain valid); if unclear, consider expression of concern and contact institutions; if authors exonerated publish correction if needed and inform complainant; keep institutions contacted every 3–6 months if unresolved. Note: this flowchart relates only to digital photographic images; for wider data fabrication consult other flowcharts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism in a submitted manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps when a reviewer/editor identifies suspected plagiarism in a submitted manuscript.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank reviewer and gather documentary evidence; check degree of copying and classify as clear plagiarism (large unattributed text/data), redundancy (self-plagiarism), or minor copying of short phrases; for minor copying request rephrasing or proper quotations and references, discuss with reviewer and proceed with review; for clear plagiarism contact corresponding author enclosing authorship statement and documentary evidence, ask for explanation — if unsatisfactory reject manuscript and consider informing author’s superior and/or person responsible for research governance and potential victims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism in a published article
rubrics_metrics.description: Handling allegations of plagiarism in a published article raised by a reader or third party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank complainant, get documentary evidence, check degree of copying; contact corresponding author with evidence and request explanation; if unsatisfactory or admission, consider retraction or correction, inform author's institution and potential victims, publish correction/retraction as appropriate, and inform complainant of outcome/action; if satisfactory explanation (honest error or very junior researcher), discuss revision or correction and proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: General approach to publication ethics for the editorial office
rubrics_metrics.description: High-level guidance for editorial offices on managing publication ethics and implementing COPE Core practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have a general approach and policies in place; ensure escalation procedures and communications plans exist; include clear instructions to authors (e.g., definitions of plagiarism, COI policy); obtain signed COI statements from authors and reviewers; adopt transparent authorship/contributorship policies (ICMJE, ORCID, CRediT); keep relevant flowcharts accessible and follow publisher-specific guidance; consider submitting novel cases to COPE Forum; keep records and contact institutions/authorities when required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic manipulation of the publication process
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowcharts and guidance for detecting and responding to suspected organised/systematic attempts to subvert peer review and the publication process (eg, fake reviewers, third party agencies).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess for features/patterns that suggest systematic manipulation (bogus/fake reviewer accounts, suspicious email addresses, similarity across reviewer reports, third-party agency involvement, unusually rapid/positive reviews, IP address anomalies); if probable, contact corresponding author/co-authors with evidence requesting explanation; if authors admit manipulation, consider contacting authors’ institutions and retracting affected articles and inform institutions and authors of retraction wording; if response satisfactory, consider remedial actions (organising further review, updating policies) and inform authors/institutions; when institutions unlikely to investigate, consider publishing expression of concern or retracting without institutional confirmation if integrity cannot be assured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic manipulation suspected before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific steps when potential systematic manipulation is identified during submission/review (before publication).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify suggested reviewers (use institutional emails or verified ORCID), check reviewer publication record and ability to confirm manuscript details, contact named reviewers on institutional addresses to confirm identity, check for suspicious patterns (non-institutional emails, IP anomalies), if unsatisfactory contact handling editor or the author for explanation, consider suspending peer review, inviting additional independent reviewers, reject manuscript if manipulation confirmed and inform author/institution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systematic manipulation suspected after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Steps when systematic manipulation (eg, compromised peer review) is discovered after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate patterns across affected papers, contact corresponding author and co-authors with evidence requesting explanation; if no/inconclusive response, contact authors’ institutions requesting investigation and keep contacting every 3 months; consider post-publication actions such as retraction, expression of concern, or corrections depending on findings and whether conclusions remain valid; inform readers, authors, and institutions of outcomes and consider updating policies to prevent recurrence.

rubrics_metrics.name: What to consider when asked to peer review a manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Infographic/flowchart for potential reviewers deciding whether to accept an invitation to review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check whether journal is legitimate (thinkchecksubmit.org); read reviewer instructions and accept only if you understand/accept the review model and policies; consider potential conflicts of interest and the journal’s CoI policy — if conflict exists discuss mitigation with editor otherwise decline; consider expertise, time to complete review and whether author information (if needed for anonymity) is provided; if double-blind and you can guess authors, consider conflicts; if unable to meet deadline or insufficient expertise, decline and suggest other reviewers; if accepting, notify editor and proceed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review manipulation suspected during the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: How editors should handle suspected manipulation of peer review while the manuscript is under review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If reviewer name appears legitimate but email suspicious, attempt to verify reviewer via institutional contact or public records; contact named reviewer using organisational email to confirm whether they used the provided email; if verification fails or explanation unsatisfactory, contact the person who suggested the reviewer (e.g., handling editor) for explanation; consider suspending peer review, invite additional reviewers, or reject manuscript if manipulation is confirmed; explain situation neutrally to authors and institutions and consider removing or blacklisting suspicious reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review manipulation suspected after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Handling peer review manipulation discovered after an article has been published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify extent of manipulation and whether other reviewers were compromised; contact named reviewer via institutional email to confirm identity and details; if publication integrity is affected and authors/institutions admit or evidence supports manipulation, consider post-publication peer review, publish expression of concern, corrections, or retract articles as appropriate; inform authors, institutions, and readers of actions taken; consider wider investigation into the peer review process and update policies to require institutional email or verified ORCID for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to recognise potential manipulation of the peer review process
rubrics_metrics.description: List of recognised features and patterns that may indicate peer review manipulation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicators include: similarity across reviewer reports purportedly from different people; third-party agency involvement; use of non-institutional email addresses (gmail, yahoo, etc); reviews that are vague or stylistically inconsistent with claimed seniority; excessively positive reviews contradicting other reviewers; reviews returned extremely quickly; reviewers who never recommend rejection; reviewers who review many manuscripts rapidly; IP address anomalies; fictitious reviewer names; reviewers working in unrelated subjects. Use combinations of these signs to prompt investigation; best practice: require institutional emails, verify suggested reviewers' qualifications, and check for unusual patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant (duplicate) publication in a submitted manuscript
rubrics_metrics.description: Flowchart for handling reviewer reports of redundant or duplicate submission (same data/publishing elsewhere).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Thank reviewer and gather documentary evidence; check extent/nature of overlap: major overlap (same data, identical findings, evidence authors tried to hide duplication) vs minor overlap (methods, re-analysis, legitimate republication); contact corresponding author with evidence and request missing references or removal of overlapping material; if satisfactory explanation (legitimate republication) proceed possibly with correction to cite original; if unsatisfactory or deliberate hiding, consider rejecting manuscript, informing author's institution and person responsible for research governance, and keep institution contact every 3–6 months if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Redundant (duplicate) publication in a published article
rubrics_metrics.description: How to handle allegations of redundancy/duplicate publication for already published articles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gather documentary evidence and assess overlap as major or minor; contact corresponding author with evidence and request explanation and/or correction referencing original work; if no response or unsatisfactory explanation and deliberate failure to cite previous work suspected, consider informing author’s institution and possibly retracting or publishing a statement of redundant publication (in coordination with other journals), inform readers of outcome and keep contacting institutions if necessary.
